title: The invention of cotton candy: spun sugar, the 1897 machine, the 1904 St. Louis fair, and sugar and tooth decay

sources.title: The sticky sweet history of cotton candy
People at the World's Fair Paid Half the Price of Admission for a Box of Cotton Candy (Kat Eschner, 2016-12-07)
Sugars and dental caries (fact sheet, 2025-08-14)
sources.note: WHO 出版品只取事實、不改寫

facts.text: Spun sugar was made by hand long before any machine existed; it goes back at least to the 1400s in Italy.
Cooks melted sugar and used a fork to pull it into thin threads, which they hung over a wooden stick.
Making spun sugar by hand was slow, hard work, so it remained a treat for rich people until the machine came along.
In 1897, William Morrison, a dentist, and John C. Wharton, a candy maker, designed an electric machine for making spun sugar.
William Morrison worked as a dentist in Nashville, Tennessee.
In the machine, a heater melts the sugar into a liquid, and a fast-spinning head pushes the liquid out through tiny holes.
The thin strands of sugar cool so quickly that they cannot form crystals again, so the sweet is a solid like glass, mostly filled with air.
Morrison and Wharton sold the sweet at the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis under the name fairy floss, packed in boxes.
At the 1904 fair, a box of fairy floss cost 25 cents, which was half the price of a ticket to enter the fair.
Morrison and Wharton sold more than 65,000 boxes of fairy floss at the 1904 fair (National Geographic gives 68,655 servings).
The 1904 fair in St. Louis lasted about seven months and drew an estimated 20 million visitors.
In the 1920s, Josef Lascaux, another dentist who sold the sweet to his patients, gave it the name cotton candy.
The same sweet is called candy floss in Britain and fairy floss in Australia.
The early machines tended to shake, rattle, overheat, and lose their balance; in 1949 a Cincinnati company added a spring-loaded base to the machine.
According to the WHO, eating and drinking free sugars is the most common risk factor for tooth decay.
Tooth decay happens when plaque on a tooth turns free sugars into acids, which slowly destroy the tooth over time.
The WHO advises keeping free sugars below 10 percent of the energy a person takes in each day, and ideally below 5 percent.
Not getting enough fluoride and not removing plaque by brushing teeth also lead to tooth decay.
About 2.5 billion people around the world have tooth decay, making it the most common disease of its kind that is not passed from person to person.

notes: 原始角度：1897 年牙醫 Morrison 與糖果師傅 Wharton 做出電動棉花糖機，1904 年聖路易世界博覽會以 fairy floss 之名販售。售出盒數兩個來源不同（Smithsonian：超過 65,000 盒；National Geographic：68,655 份），選文只寫 more than 65,000。Smithsonian 只說 25 美分是門票的一半，門票價格本身（50 美分）由此推得，選文不寫門票的數字。專利日期（1897 年申請、1899 年核准）只有白名單外的來源，事實單不列，選文只寫 1897 年設計出機器。
